title: You'll Probably Never Spend Your Retirement Savings (20,000 Retirees Prove It)

description:

Retirees who started retirement with $500,000 or more had spent only 11.8% of it nearly 20 years later (EBRI, median household). On $800,000, that is about $94,400 in two decades, while the 4% rule would allow $32,000 a year.

The Health and Retirement Study (University of Michigan) has followed about 20,000 Americans over 50 since 1992. Two results drive this video. EBRI found that retirees spend roughly what comes in, and leave savings almost untouched (median decline: about 4% with a pension, 34% without). Blanchett and Finke (April 2025) found that retirees spend about 80% of lifetime income like Social Security, around 2% a year of their savings, and less than half of their capital income, which includes dividends.

So the problem for a dividend investor is not the yield. It is the shape of the money. $800,000 in SCHD (Nov 3, 2026 close of $35.55, $1.0541 per share over 12 months, 2.97% trailing yield) paid about $23,721 a year, but in four uneven quarterly lumps. We turn that into a $1,780 monthly paycheck with a six-month buffer, stress-test it against 2009 (S&P 500 dividends -21.4%), map it to fixed and flexible bills, run the 2026 federal tax for a married couple, and ask what three more years of work actually buy.
